title: From Bean to Bar: The Making of Chocolate
body_html:
Chocolate begins its life on a tree that refuses to behave like most crops. Theobroma cacao — the 'food of the gods', as the botanist Linnaeus named it — grows only within about twenty degrees of the equator, and even there it is fussy. It is a delicate understorey tree that prefers the shade of taller neighbours to full, direct sunlight, and it produces its fruit in a way botanists call cauliflory: the flowers, and later the pods, sprout directly from the trunk and the thickest branches rather than from young twigs. A mature pod is about the size of a small rugby ball. It has a thick, ridged husk that turns from green to yellow, orange or crimson as it ripens, and it hangs from the trunk on a short woody stalk. Split one open and you will find thirty to fifty seeds — the cocoa beans — embedded in a layer of sweet white pulp. Ripe pods never fall from the tree of their own accord, and they must be cut by hand, usually with a machete or a curved knife on a pole, because a careless blow from a machine would destroy the cushions of tissue on the trunk from which new flowers, and therefore future harvests, grow.

A raw cocoa bean is a disappointment: fresh from the pod it is astringent and so bitter as to be inedible, with none of the flavour we associate with chocolate. That flavour has to be created, and the first and most important step is fermentation. On the farm, the beans and their clinging pulp are scooped out of the pods, heaped into wooden boxes or onto mats, covered with banana leaves and left for about six days. Wild yeasts and bacteria feed on the sugary pulp, which liquefies and drains away, and the temperature inside the heap climbs steeply. In this brief, violent chemistry the harshest compounds in the bean begin to break down and the precursors of chocolate flavour are formed. Beans that skip this stage never taste of chocolate, however skilfully they are processed later.

Fermentation leaves the beans far too wet to store, so they are next spread out in shallow layers on mats or raised tables and dried in the sun for around a week. Workers turn them regularly with wooden rakes so that they dry evenly and do not grow mould, and the moisture content falls from roughly sixty per cent to about seven. Only then are the beans bagged, graded and shipped, most often to factories on the other side of the world.

At the factory the flavour is coaxed further by roasting, which browns the beans and drives off the sharpest remaining acids. The roasted beans then pass through a winnowing machine: rollers crack them open, and the loose shells, being far lighter than the kernels, are blown away by fans, leaving behind broken fragments of pure bean known as nibs.

The nibs are then ground between steel rollers or stones. More than half of a nib's weight is fat — cocoa butter — and the heat of grinding melts it, so that what emerges is not a powder but a thick, flowing paste known as cocoa liquor. Sugar, extra cocoa butter and, for milk chocolate, dried milk are blended in, and the mixture then undergoes the strangest stage of all: conching. Invented by Rodolphe Lindt in 1879, the conche kneads and aerates the warm chocolate, in some factories for as long as three days, until the gritty particles are ground too small for the tongue to detect and the last harsh flavours evaporate; the purpose of conching, in short, is to make the chocolate smooth. Finally the liquid chocolate is tempered: it is carefully cooled and then gently reheated so that stable crystals of cocoa butter form throughout it. Well-tempered chocolate sets glossy and hard and breaks with a clean snap; badly tempered chocolate is dull, crumbly and streaked with grey.

For all the machinery at the factory end, the crop itself remains stubbornly a smallholder's plant. The great majority of the world's cocoa is grown not on large plantations but on family smallholdings of a few hectares, and two West African countries, Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana, together supply well over half of the global harvest. The tree's demands — shade, heat, humidity and endless hand labour — have so far defeated most attempts to mechanise the harvest. The bar that snaps so neatly in a European or American shop is, from the first cut of the machete to the final fold of foil, a product that still begins with a farmer, a knife and a tree that fruits from its trunk.

title: The Trombe Wall: Heating Buildings with Sunlight
body_html:
On a hillside at Odeillo, in the French Pyrenees, stands a row of houses whose southern faces are almost entirely dark glass. They were built in the 1960s by the engineer Félix Trombe and the architect Jacques Michel, and they heat themselves, in large part, with nothing more elaborate than a wall. The idea was not strictly new — a patent for a glazed, sun-warmed wall had been granted to the American inventor Edward Morse as early as 1881, and promptly forgotten — but it was Trombe and Michel who turned the curiosity into a working system, and it is Trombe's name the design now bears. The Trombe wall belongs to the family of 'passive' solar designs, which are distinguished from solar panels and heat pumps by having no moving parts, no fluids to circulate and nothing that draws electricity: the building itself is the machine.

The construction is disarmingly simple. On the side of the building that faces the winter sun — the south side, in the northern hemisphere — a massive wall is built of brick, stone or concrete, materials chosen for their capacity to store large quantities of heat. Its outer face is coated with matt black paint so that it absorbs as much sunlight as possible, and a sheet of glazing, of single or double glass, is fixed a few centimetres in front of it, sealing off a narrow cavity of trapped air. Rows of vents pierce the wall near the ceiling and near the floor, connecting this cavity to the room behind.

During a winter day the wall works as a slow engine of circulation. Sunlight passes through the glazing and strikes the black surface, which absorbs the radiation; the glass, meanwhile, prevents the resulting warmth from escaping — the same trapping of heat that makes the inside of a parked car so uncomfortable in summer. The air in the cavity can reach sixty degrees Celsius. Being hot, it rises, and streams into the room through the upper vents, while cooler air near the floor of the room is drawn out through the lower vents into the bottom of the cavity to be heated in its turn. The result is a continuous convective loop — engineers call it a thermosiphon — that carries warmth into the building all afternoon without a single fan.

The wall's second act begins at sunset. Masonry conducts heat slowly: warmth absorbed at the outer face takes several hours to creep through to the inner one, and this time lag is precisely what makes the design valuable. Heat collected at midday reaches the interior surface in the evening, just as the outside temperature is falling and the rooms most need it, and the wall then radiates gently into the room for much of the night. Two precautions are essential. The vents must be closed after dark; otherwise the circulation reverses, and air chilled against the cold glass sinks and pours back into the room. In careful designs an insulated shutter is also lowered over the glazing at night, cutting the heat that would otherwise be lost back through the glass. Summer brings the opposite problem, and the classic remedy is architectural rather than mechanical: a projecting roof overhang above the glazing shades the wall from the high summer sun while leaving it exposed to the low sun of winter, and additional vents at the top of the cavity can be opened to the outside so that unwanted hot air is dumped there rather than indoors.

How well does it all work? The honest answer is that it depends where you build. In regions where winter skies are reliably clear — mountain plateaux, high deserts, much of the Mediterranean — a well-proportioned Trombe wall can supply a substantial share of a house's winter heating, and studies of the Odeillo houses themselves reported savings of that order. In persistently cloudy regions the case is far weaker, for a wall that receives little sun spends much of the winter as nothing more than a poorly insulated slab of cold masonry. Nor is money the design's real attraction: a Trombe wall is not especially cheap to build, and its appeal lies less in economy than in simplicity and endurance — there is nothing to break down, nothing to service and nothing to replace. It will never match the glamour of the photovoltaic roof, but as a means of letting a building heat itself, quietly and for decades, it has few rivals.

questions.prompt_text: Flow-chart gap 2 — The dark surface absorbs the radiation, heating the air trapped in the narrow ______.
questions.evidence: Paragraph 2 explains the glazing seals off "a narrow cavity of trapped air", and paragraph 3 says the air in this cavity can reach sixty degrees.

questions.prompt_text: Flow-chart gap 3 — The hot air rises and streams into the room through the ______.
questions.evidence: Paragraph 3 states the hot air "rises, and streams into the room through the upper vents".

questions.prompt_text: Flow-chart gap 4 — Cooler air near the floor is drawn back to be heated again, forming a continuous ______.
questions.evidence: Paragraph 3 calls the result "a continuous convective loop — engineers call it a thermosiphon".

questions.prompt_text: Diagram label 1 — a projecting roof ______ that shades the glass from the high summer sun
questions.evidence: Paragraph 4 describes "a projecting roof overhang above the glazing" that shades the wall from the high summer sun.

questions.prompt_text: Diagram label 2 — an insulated ______ that is lowered over the glass after dark
questions.evidence: Paragraph 4 says "an insulated shutter is also lowered over the glazing at night" to cut heat losses through the glass.

questions.prompt_text: Diagram label 3 — the coating of matt ______ on the outer face of the wall
questions.evidence: Paragraph 2 says the outer face "is coated with matt black paint so that it absorbs as much sunlight as possible".

questions.prompt_text: Diagram label 4 — a massive wall built of brick, stone or ______
questions.evidence: Paragraph 2 states the wall is "built of brick, stone or concrete, materials chosen for their capacity to store large quantities of heat".

questions.prompt_text: Why does the design bear Félix Trombe's name?
questions.evidence: Paragraph 1 notes Edward Morse patented the idea in 1881 but it was "promptly forgotten", and that Trombe and Michel "turned the curiosity into a working system".

questions.prompt_text: According to the passage, the vents must be closed at night
questions.evidence: Paragraph 4 warns that otherwise "the circulation reverses, and air chilled against the cold glass sinks and pours back into the room".

options.text: It stores heat from the summer for use in winter.
It prevents the cavity from becoming too hot.
It delivers warmth indoors in the evening, when it is most needed.

questions.prompt_text: Why is the wall's time lag described as valuable?
questions.evidence: Paragraph 4 says heat collected at midday "reaches the interior surface in the evening, just as the outside temperature is falling and the rooms most need it".

questions.prompt_text: A Trombe wall is a poor choice in places where winters are consistently cloudy.
questions.evidence: Paragraph 5 says that in persistently cloudy regions "the case is far weaker", the wall becoming little more than a poorly insulated slab of cold masonry.

questions.prompt_text: The main attraction of a Trombe wall is its low construction cost.
questions.evidence: Paragraph 5 states a Trombe wall "is not especially cheap to build, and its appeal lies less in economy than in simplicity and endurance".

questions.prompt_text: Governments ought to encourage passive solar design in new housing.
questions.evidence: The writer assesses where the design works well but expresses no view about government policy or encouragement.
